questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows the graph of
$$y=1-\log_{10}(\sin x) \qquad 0<x<\pi$$
where $x$ is in radians.
The table below shows some values of $x$ and $y$ for this graph, with values of $y$ given to 3 decimal places.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 0.5 & 1 & 1.5 & 2 & 2.5 & 3\\ \hline y & 1.319 & & 1.001 & & 1.223 & 1.850\\ \hline\end{array}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Complete the table above, giving values of $y$ to 3 decimal places.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Either of awrt 1.075 or awrt 1.041 correct
B1: Both of awrt 1.075 and awrt 1.041 correct
Note that the incorrect values of 2.758 and 2.457 come from the use of degrees.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Remember to check the body of the script for the values if the table has not been completed. (Which gives 4.51 in (b))

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Use the trapezium rule with all the $y$ values in the completed table to find, to 2 decimal places, an estimate for
$$\int_{0.5}^{3}\left(1-\log_{10}(\sin x)\right)\mathrm{d}x$$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $h=0.5$ seen or implied
M1: Area $\approx\left\{\frac{0.5}{2}\right\}\times\left(1.319+2("1.075"+1.001+"1.041"+1.223)+1.850\right)$ Correct application of the trapezium rule. Must all be $y$ values, first + last + 2(sum of middle values), but if one middle value is omitted allow as a slip. A repeated value is M0. Follow through their values from (a). Allow obvious copying slips.
A1: $=$ awrt 2.96. Allow to come from answers in (a) incorrectly rounded or wrong accuracy.
Official notes (completeness pass):

parts.label: c
parts.text:

$$\int_{0.5}^{3}\left(3+\log_{10}(\sin x)\right)\mathrm{d}x$$
(3)

parts.label: i
parts.text:
(i) Show that the following statement is false:
"$(n+1)^3-n^3$ is prime for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$"
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: E.g. $n=1: 2^3-1^3=7$, $n=2: 3^3-2^3=19$, $n=3: 4^3-3^3=\ldots$ Or identifies counterexample directly. Shows evidence of trying to find a counter example for a positive integer (at least one attempt). $2^3-1^3$ is prime is sufficient.
A1: e.g. $6^3-5^3=91=7\times13$ so not true for $n=5$, hence statement is not true. Gives a correct counter example with reason (shows factorisation) and concludes e.g. "which is not prime". Ignore any previous "incorrect" attempts e.g. $6^3-5^3=91$ which is prime. Note $n=7$ (169=13$\times$13) and $n=8$ (217=7$\times$31) and $n=12$ (469=7$\times$67) are the next few counter examples. Allow equivalent reasons for not being prime e.g. 169/13=13 or 169 is divisible by 13 (condone "can be divided by 13"). Generally algebraic approaches score no marks unless they substitute numbers as indicated above.

parts.label: ii
parts.text:
(ii) Given that the points $A(1,0)$, $B(3,-10)$ and $C(7,-6)$ lie on a circle, prove that $AB$ is a diameter of this circle.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
The majority of methods here will follow ways 1, 2 or 3 below. In these cases the general guidance is as follows:
M1: Attempts to find the gradient of any relevant line, e.g. AC or BC, or the length of any relevant line, e.g. AB/AB^2 or BC/BC^2 or AC/AC^2, or the mid-point M of line AB.
A1: Correct relevant calculation of gradients AC and BC, or lengths of lines AB/AB^2, BC/BC^2 and AC/AC^2, or mid-point of line AB.
dM1: Full attempt at combining all relevant information required to solve the problem — attempts product of gradients or equivalent, or attempts to show Pythagoras $AB^2=AC^2+BC^2$, or attempts to show $MA^2=MC^2$.
A1: Correct calculations or equivalent providing required evidence for the above.
A1: Provides correct reason and conclusion with all previous marks scored.
Way 1: $m_{AC}=\frac{-6-0}{7-1}=\ldots$ or $m_{BC}=\frac{-6-(-10)}{7-3}=\ldots$ (M1); $m_{AC}=-1$ and $m_{BC}=1$ (A1); So $m_{AC}\times m_{BC}=-1\times1=-1$ or e.g. $m_{AC}$ is negative reciprocal of $m_{BC}$ (dM1A1); So e.g. angle (at C) is a right angle hence AB is a diameter (or equivalent) (A1).
Way 2: $AB=\sqrt{(3-1)^2+(-10-0)^2}=\ldots$ or $AC=\sqrt{(7-1)^2+(-6-0)^2}=\ldots$ or $BC=\sqrt{(7-3)^2+(-6+10)^2}=\ldots$ (M1); $AB=\sqrt{104}(2\sqrt{26})$, $AC=\sqrt{72}(6\sqrt{2})$, $BC=\sqrt{32}(4\sqrt{2})$ (A1); $AB^2=104=72+32=AC^2+BC^2$ (dM1A1); Hence ABC is a right-angle triangle with hypotenuse AB hence AB is a diameter. (or equivalent) (A1).
Way 3: If AB is diameter centre must be midpoint of AB ie $M\left(\frac{1+3}{2},\frac{0-10}{2}\right)$ (M1); $=(2,-5)$ (A1); $MA=\sqrt{(2-1)^2+(-5-0)^2}=\sqrt{26}$, $MC=\sqrt{(2-7)^2+(-5-(-6))^2}=\sqrt{26}$ (dM1A1); $MA=\sqrt{26}, MC=\sqrt{26}$ so $MA=MC(=MB)$; As the length from M to each of A and C is the same M is the centre of the circle hence AB is a diameter. (Or equivalent) (A1).
Way 4: If AB is diameter centre must be midpoint of AB ie $M(2,-5)$ (M1A1); $MA=r=\sqrt{(2-1)^2+(-5-0)^2}=\sqrt{26}\Rightarrow(x-2)^2+(y+5)^2=26$; $C(7,-6)\Rightarrow(7-2)^2+(-6+5)^2=5^2+1^2=26$ (dM1A1); As C also satisfies the equation of the circle then AB must be the diameter (or equivalent) — there must be some further justification as above rather than just "AB is a diameter" which may be in a preamble e.g. If C lies on the circle... (A1). There may be other methods; choose the way that best fits the overall response.

- Way 2 M1: Attempts length of AB or AC or BC or their squares. Allow slips but score M0 if attempts are clearly incorrect. dM1: Applies Pythagoras' theorem with their values. (May see cosine rule used.)
- Way 3 M1: Attempts midpoint of AB. If no method is shown accept one correct coordinate as evidence. dM1: Attempts length of MC and at least one of MA or MB, or AB. A1: Suitable explanation made which may be in a preamble and conclusion given with no errors and all previous marks awarded.
- Way 4 dM1: Attempts length of MA or MB to find r or $r^2$, forms equation of the circle and substitutes the coordinates of C. If you are in any doubt if a particular response deserves credit then use Review.
- Way 5 (via perpendicular bisectors): If AB is diameter centre must be midpoint of AB ie $M\left(\frac{1+3}{2},\frac{0-10}{2}\right)$ M1; $=(2,-5)$ A1; Attempts 2 of: $m_{BC}=\frac{-6+10}{7-3}=1$ and midpoint is $(5,-8)$ so perpendicular bisector is $y+"8"=-\frac{1}{"1"}(x-"5")$ or $m_{AC}=-1$ and midpoint is $(4,-3)$ so perpendicular bisector is $y+"3"=-\frac{1}{"-1"}(x-"4")$ or $m_{AB}=\frac{-10-0}{3-1}=-5$ and midpoint is $(2,-5)$ so perpendicular bisector is $y+"5"=-\frac{1}{"-5"}(x-"2")$; $y+8=-(x-5)$ oe or $y+3=x-4$ oe or $y+5=\frac15(x-2)$ oe And solves simultaneously: E.g. $y+3=x-4, y+8=5-x\Rightarrow5-x-5=x-4\Rightarrow x=2,y=-5$ dM1; Hence centre of circle is $(2,-5)$ A1; E.g. Midpoint of AB is the centre of the circle so AB is a diameter (or equivalent) A1. dM1: Attempts 2 perpendicular bisectors, and solves simultaneously. A1: Obtains (2, −5)
- Way 6 (via circle equation): Uses $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$ With (1, 0), (7, −6) and (3, −10) To find (a, b) = … or r/r$^2$ = … M1; Centre $(2,-5)$ or radius $\sqrt{26}$ A1; E.g. Equation of AB is $y=-5(x-1)$ and $-5(2-1)=-5$ or $AB=\sqrt{(3-1)^2+(-10-0)^2}=\sqrt{104}=2\sqrt{26}$ or midpoint of AB is $(2,-5)$ dM1A1; So centre is on AB or AB is twice the radius or midpoint is the centre hence AB is a diameter of the circle. (or equivalent) A1. M1: Uses all three points in circle equation to set up three equations in three unknowns to find centre or radius. A1: Correct centre or correct radius. dM1: Finds e.g. equation of AB, distance AB or midpoint of AB. A1: Correct equation of AB, distance AB or midpoint of AB.
- Way 7 (via intersecting circles): $M\left(\frac{1+3}{2},\frac{0-10}{2}\right)$ M1; $=(2,-5)$ A1; Circle centre C radius r is $(x-7)^2+(y+6)^2=r^2$, Circle centre B radius r is $(x-3)^2+(y+10)^2=r^2$, These intersect when $(x-7)^2+(y+6)^2=(x-3)^2+(y+10)^2\Rightarrow x+y=-3$; Circle centre A radius r is $(x-1)^2+y^2=r^2$, $(x-3)^2+(y+10)^2=(x-1)^2+y^2\Rightarrow x-5y=27$; Solves simultaneously: $x+y=-3, x-5y=27\Rightarrow x=2,y=-5$ dM1A1; E.g. Midpoint of AB is the centre of the circle so AB is a diameter (or equivalent) A1. dM1: Attempts equations of 2 circles with A, B or C as centre with radius r, repeats the process for 2 different circles and finds the intersection of both straight lines and solves simultaneously. A1: Correct coordinates of centre

questions.stem:
A scientist is using carbon-14 dating to determine the age of some wooden items.
The equation for carbon-14 dating an item is given by
$$N=k\lambda^t$$
where
• $N$ grams is the amount of carbon-14 currently present in the item
• $k$ grams was the initial amount of carbon-14 present in the item
• $t$ is the number of years since the item was made
• $\lambda$ is a constant, with $0<\lambda<1$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Sketch the graph of $N$ against $t$ for $k=1$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Correct shape from or passing through a point on positive vertical axis. May extend to the left of the vertical axis and allow to pass into quadrant 4. There must be no (obvious) turning points. Labels not required on axes and ignore any that are given.
A1: Shape and position correct, accept 1 or k as intercept on the positive vertical axis and allow to extend to the left of the vertical axis as shown. Condone $(1,0)$ or $(k,0)$ as long as it is in the correct position. The curve should approach a horizontal asymptote that is half-way between the horizontal axis and the intercept or below. Be tolerant with "wobbles" as it approaches the asymptote. May just "touch" the horizontal axis but not go below it. Labels not required on axes and ignore any that are given.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that it takes 5700 years for the amount of carbon-14 to reduce to half its initial value,
(b) show that the value of the constant $\lambda$ is 0.999878 to 6 decimal places.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\frac{1}{2}k=k\lambda^{5700}\Rightarrow\lambda^{5700}=\frac{1}{2}$ (see notes for method via substitution). Uses the information to set up a correct equation and rearranges to form $\lambda^a=b$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Allow $\lambda^{5700}=\frac12$ to be written down directly.
A1*: $\Rightarrow\lambda=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{5700}}=0.999878$ to 6 d.p. Evidence of taking fractional root seen, leading to the given answer. Alternatively, may see logs used, $5700\log\lambda=\log\frac12\Rightarrow\log\lambda=\frac{-\log2}{5700}\Rightarrow\lambda=10^{\frac{-\log2}{5700}}=\ldots$. Look for at least one correct intermediate step (and no incorrect ones). Allow greater accuracy e.g. 0.9998784026... Note that the use of 5699 instead of 5700 scores M1A0. Alt: M1: Substitutes values 0.9998775 and 0.9998785 or a tighter range containing the root (e.g. 0.999878 and 0.9998785 will do) to calculate N or just $\lambda^t$ at $t=5700$. A1*: Correct values, with suitable conclusion that as half value occurs between these $\lambda=0.999878$ to 6 d.p.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that Item $A$
• is known to have had 15 grams of carbon-14 present initially
• is thought to be 3250 years old
(c) calculate, to 3 significant figures, how much carbon-14 the equation predicts is currently in Item $A$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: When $t=3250$, $N=15\times0.999878^{3250}=\ldots$. Substitutes given values (or more accurate $\lambda$) into the equation and evaluates. Implied by a correct answer, but an incorrect answer with no evidence is M0. Allow 3249 for 3250. Condone the use of a less accurate $\lambda$ e.g. 0.9999 if the intention is clear.
A1: $=$ awrt 10.1 (grams). Units not required. Answer only can score both marks.

parts.label: d
parts.text:

(d) Use algebra to calculate the age of Item $B$ to the nearest 100 years.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $18=25\times0.999878^t$. Sets up the correct equation from the information given. It must be clear they are using the given $\lambda$ or better accuracy so clear use of e.g. 0.9999 scores B0 but allow the M1 below. This may be implied if they write e.g. $18=25\times\lambda^t$ and then go on to use the given value of $\lambda$. Allow this mark if a different letter is used for t as long as the equation is correct.

The circle $C$ has centre $X(3,5)$ and radius $r$
The line $l$ has equation $y=2x+k$, where $k$ is a constant.
(a) Show that $l$ and $C$ intersect when
$$5x^2+(4k-26)x+k^2-10k+34-r^2=0$$
(3)
Given that $l$ is a tangent to $C$,
(b) show that $5r^2=(k+p)^2$, where $p$ is a constant to be found.
(3)
The line $l$
• cuts the $y$-axis at the point $A$
• touches the circle $C$ at the point $B$
as shown in Figure 2.
Given that $AB=2r$
(c) find the value of $k$
(6)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
M1: Equation of circle is $(x-3)^2+(y-5)^2=r^2$ and line is $y=2x+k$. So intersect when $(x-3)^2+(2x+k-5)^2=r^2$. Forms equation of circle and substitutes in equation of line. The circle equation must be of the form $(x\pm3)^2+(y\pm5)^2=r^2$.
dM1: $\Rightarrow x^2-6x+9+4x^2+4(k-5)x+(k-5)^2=r^2\Rightarrow5x^2+(-6+4k-20)x+9+k^2-10k+25-r^2=0$. Expands both sets of brackets and collects terms in $x^2$ and $x$.
A1*: $\Rightarrow5x^2+(4k-26)x+k^2-10k+34-r^2=0$. Reaches the answer given with no errors seen. Note that some candidates expand the brackets first before substitution; this implies the first M and then the second M will score when terms in $x^2$ and $x$ are collected. Note about poor squaring e.g. $(x-3)^2=x^2+9$: the first M is available in both cases above but the second M requires at least two $x^2$ terms and at least two $x$ terms from the expansions. Note that it is acceptable to go from a completely correct full expansion to the printed answer, scoring full marks in (a).
M1: Tangent to $C\Rightarrow b^2-4ac=0\Rightarrow(4k-26)^2-4\times5\times(k^2-10k+34-r^2)=0$. Uses the discriminant is zero to form an equation in $k$ and $r$.
M1: $\Rightarrow16k^2-208k+676-20k^2+200k-680+20r^2=0\Rightarrow5r^2=\ldots$. Expands and rearranges to make $\alpha r^2$ the subject.
A1: $\Rightarrow5r^2=k^2+2k+1=(k+1)^2$. Correct answer.
Way 2: M1: Gradient of BX is $-\frac{1}{2}$ so equation of BX is $y-5=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)$; $y-5=-\frac12(x-3), y=2x+k\Rightarrow x=\ldots, y=\ldots\left(\frac{13-2k}{5},\frac{26+k}{5}\right)$. Attempts the equation of BX and solves simultaneously with $l$ to find the coordinates of B. Alternatively uses $x=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{13-2k}{5}$ at B and uses this to find $y$ at B.
dM1: $\left(\frac{13-2k}{5}-3\right)^2+\left(\frac{26+k}{5}-5\right)^2=r^2$. Correct use of Pythagoras for BX and sets $=r^2$.
A1: $\Rightarrow5r^2=k^2+2k+1=(k+1)^2$. Correct answer.
M1: Triangle AXB is right angled so $AB^2+r^2=XA^2=(3-0)^2+(5-k)^2$. Attempts $XA^2$ correctly in terms of $k$ (the $k$ may appear as $y$ but must be replaced by $k$ later) and uses it in Pythagoras theorem for triangle AXB. May be implied.
M1: $AB^2=4r^2$ so $AB^2+r^2=5r^2$. Applies $AB=2r$ to get $AB^2+r^2$ in terms of $r$. Condone with $AB^2=2r^2$ used.
A1: $\Rightarrow5r^2=9+(5-k)^2$. Correct equation.
M1: $\Rightarrow k^2+2k+1=9+25-10k+k^2$. Substitutes the result from (b) and expands brackets.
dM1: $\Rightarrow12k=33\Rightarrow k=\ldots$. Solves a linear equation in $k$. Depends on the previous M.
A1: $k=\frac{11}{4}$. Correct value.
Alt (c): M1: At B $x=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{13-2k}{5}, y=2\left(\frac{13-2k}{5}\right)+k$. Uses the result in (a) to find the x coordinate where the line and circle meet and then finds y. An alternative is to find the equation of BX as in (b) way 2 and solve with l to find x and y at B (may have already found the coordinates of B in (a) but must be re-stated or used in (c) to score this mark).
M1A1: $AB^2=\left(\frac{13-2k}{5}-0\right)^2+\left(\frac{26-4k}{5}+k-k\right)^2$. Uses distance formula to find an expression in $k$ for AB or $AB^2$. Correct expression for AB or $AB^2$, need not be simplified.
M1: $\Rightarrow25\times4r^2=(13-2k)^2+(26-4k)^2=\ldots$. Applies $AB=2r$ to the equation. Condone with $AB^2=2r^2$ used.
dM1: $\Rightarrow20\times(k+1)^2=(13-2k)^2+(26-4k)^2=20k^2-260k+845\Rightarrow k^2+2k+1=k^2-13k+\frac{169}{4}\Rightarrow k=\ldots$. Substitutes the result from (b) and solves a linear equation in $k$. Depends on the previous M.
A1: $\Rightarrow k=\frac{11}{4}$. Correct value.
